soil-bio-193.title: Nematodes, the most numerous animals on Earth
soil-bio-193.text: Earth's topsoil holds about 4.4 × 10^20 nematodes, roughly 60 billion for every person. Nematodes are roundworms, or eelworms, the animal phylum Nematoda. Most live freely and feed on microbes, but many are parasites. They often exceed a million individuals per square meter, and they make up about 80% of all individual animals on Earth. Densities peak in tundra and boreal forests. About 90% of soil nematodes live in the top 15 cm. They do not break down dead material. They eat living things instead, up to 5,000 bacteria per minute, and so regulate bacterial numbers and the mix of bacterial kinds. By releasing nitrogen in mineral form, they can play an important part in the movement of nitrogen through soil. They are prey too: nematophagous fungi trap them with lassos or sticky structures, or release toxins on contact. Species are hard to tell apart, so estimates of their number run from over 25,000 to close to one million. The soil-dwelling Caenorhabditis elegans is a major model organism. In 2023 a Panagrolaimus kolymaensis was revived after 46,000 years in Siberian permafrost.

soil-bio-194.title: Plant-parasitic nematodes, the hidden thieves of crops
soil-bio-194.text: Each year about 10% of the world's crops are lost to worms too small to see. Plant-parasitic nematodes attack crop plants, chiefly their roots, or spread plant viruses between them. Major kinds include root-knot Meloidogyne, cyst-forming Globodera and Heterodera, and lesion-causing Pratylenchus. Root-knot species leave visible galls on roots, a field clue for diagnosis. Others, such as Xiphinema index, carry viruses. Farmers fight back with rotations of resistant crops, marigolds grown between crops and antagonistic fungi and bacteria. In CSIRO plots, Brassica juncea worked into the soil while green cut densities 13- to 14-fold. Soil steaming kills them before planting, but it also kills the beneficial soil fauna.

soil-bio-195.title: Testate amoebae, single cells that carry a shell
soil-bio-195.text: Some single cells build their own houses. Testate amoebae are amoeboid protists partly enclosed in a shell, or test, with an opening for their pseudopodia, flowing arm-like extensions. The cell either makes the test itself, from organic, siliceous or calcareous material, or glues it together from mineral grains. They live in most fresh waters, soils and {{ref:soil-water-137}}. In soil the shell guards against drying, and they may stay encysted until conditions improve. Tests outlast their makers. Some species respond to temperature, pH and conductivity, so their shells serve as bioindicators and records of past climate, and of land-use change during soil formation.
